title: Platform Governance, Portability & Dependency Atlas
purpose: Study online platforms as governance and dependency systems: who sets rules, how visibility and moderation operate, what users can carry elsewhere, and where creators or communities become structurally dependent.

questions: Object removal, reach reduction, account restriction, demonetization, age/geographic gating or other measures?
Can a user challenge a decision?
Is there a reason code, evidence, timeline and independent review?
Which distribution systems matter: following, search, recommendation, trending, notifications?
Which criteria are known, inferred or opaque?
Who controls payouts, advertising eligibility, subscriptions, donations, commerce or sponsorship tools?
Can users retrieve content, metadata, contact graph, subscribers/followers, account history or moderation history?
Can identity, audience, content or social graph move across services?
Which courts, regulators, auditors, researchers or public reporting systems can inspect the platform?

dependency_vector.measure: share of reachable audience concentrated on one platform
share of creator/community income dependent on one platform
degree to which reputation/account identity cannot be moved
degree to which history/content disappears if the service closes or access is lost
share of discovery controlled by platform-owned ranking
dependence on platform-specific production, community or moderation tools
ability to export/reconstruct follower, subscription or community relationships
ability to participate or publish across multiple platforms without prohibitive cost

resilience_patterns: portable archives preserve memory even when reach is lost
open protocols can reduce identity/audience lock-in but do not automatically solve moderation or abuse
creator-owned mailing lists/domains/archives can preserve direct reach
platform dependence can be high even when formal exit is technically easy
boundary_rules: Removal or reduced reach is not automatically censorship in the legal sense; jurisdiction and actor matter.
Opaque ranking does not prove intentional suppression of a particular person or viewpoint.
High engagement does not prove algorithmic favoritism without stronger evidence.
Platform migration can change governance, incentives and community composition at the same time.

concrete_cases.observed_mechanism: W3C ActivityPub defines client-to-server and federated server-to-server social networking APIs using ActivityStreams 2.0, allowing independently implemented services to exchange social objects and notifications.

portability_dimensions.social_graph: interoperable following/federation patterns depend on implementation
portability_dimensions.provider_exit: not equivalent to seamless account migration

concrete_cases.research_value: Separates interoperability from true account portability: services can communicate without guaranteeing that one user's identity, history and graph migrate intact between providers.
concrete_cases.boundary: Federation reduces some platform isolation but does not by itself solve moderation, abuse, archival continuity, discoverability or provider-switching costs.

concrete_cases.observed_mechanism: AT Protocol uses persistent decentralized identifiers and signed repositories so identity can remain stable while the hosting Personal Data Server changes; official documentation describes account migration to a new PDS.

portability_dimensions.identity: designed to remain stable across services/providers
portability_dimensions.content: signed repository designed to move with account
portability_dimensions.social_graph: protocol design explicitly aims to preserve graph across provider change
portability_dimensions.provider_exit: migration supported; recovery/migration mechanics can evolve

concrete_cases.research_value: A stronger portability case than simple export because the design tries to preserve live identity and social continuity, not only hand the user a static archive.
concrete_cases.boundary: Official migration guidance notes that specific migration mechanisms are not themselves a fixed formal protocol surface and may evolve.

concrete_cases.observed_mechanism: Google lets users create downloadable archives across products including Gmail, Drive/Docs, Calendar, Photos, YouTube videos and account activity.

portability_dimensions.identity: export does not transfer live Google identity
portability_dimensions.content: many user-held records can be exported
portability_dimensions.provider_exit: archive helps preservation/transfer but does not guarantee destination-service reconstruction

concrete_cases.research_value: Shows the difference between data portability as export and service portability as continuity of identity, graph, ranking history, moderation state and audience access.
concrete_cases.boundary: Downloading data does not itself delete the source copy, and an export being available does not mean another platform can fully reconstruct the originating service state.

concrete_cases.observed_mechanism: YouTube documents warnings, strikes, removals, restrictions and creator appeals. Its transparency documentation says appeals and reinstatements are included in Community Guidelines enforcement reporting, while some restriction types are not included in that report.

portability_dimensions.content: removed/restricted content may become unavailable on-platform
portability_dimensions.provider_exit: appeal concerns enforcement inside YouTube, not migration

concrete_cases.research_value: Provides a concrete case for measuring notice, sanction type, appeal availability, reversal/reinstatement and transparency-report scope.
concrete_cases.boundary: An appeal is a review mechanism but not independent external adjudication; reporting coverage must be checked before using platform transparency totals as a complete enforcement census.

case_method: For each platform/protocol, distinguish interoperability, export, migration, identity continuity and audience continuity. Do not use the word portability without naming which object actually moves.
